title: RTM
summary: RTM is a financially motivated criminal operation documented in public reporting from around the middle of the last decade, when researchers described a banking trojan family distributed mainly to Russian-speaking users. The group used email lures and, notably, abused legitimate remote administration software so that its traffic blended with ordinary IT support activity. Reporting describes a small, organised team that monitored its own infections, adapted malware to interfere with security products, and aimed at accounting and finance staff rather than the general public. Evidence appears in unexpected remote administration sessions, new persistence entries and outbound connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure. A common misunderstanding is that remote administration tools are inherently malicious; here the tool is legitimate and the misuse is the signal. Because the core public reporting is dated, current activity should be described only from recent sources.

beginner.definition: RTM is the name of both a criminal group and the banking malware it used. Public reports describe it targeting people who speak Russian, especially those who handle money at work. Instead of writing every tool itself, the group used legal remote support software. That made its activity look like normal technical help.
beginner.whyItMatters: When criminals use legal tools, your security software may not raise an alarm at all. Money loss is the direct result, but stolen accounting access also lets them send fake payment requests to suppliers. Small finance teams are often the target, because they hold the keys to company payments. If nobody checks remote support sessions, an intruder can look like a helpful technician. Simple process, such as calling back to confirm, blocks many of these losses.
howItWorks: A victim receives an email with a document or link connected to fake financial paperwork.
Opening it installs malware that hides itself and starts again with the computer.
The malware watches the browser and quietly changes payment details during online banking.
The group also installs legal remote support software to keep manual control of the machine.
Stolen data goes to attacker servers over the same network ports normal support tools use.
Operators keep changing the malware so that security products stop recognising it over time.
beginner.example: Think of an office where the IT team fixes laptops by connecting from another city. Nobody questions a support session, because that is normal here. Now imagine a criminal borrows the same support software and connects at midnight. The screen looks identical to a normal session. RTM works like that. The disguise is not a fake badge, it is the real, familiar tool everyone already trusts.
takeaways: Legitimate remote support software can hide criminal activity.
Confirm money transfers and support sessions through a second channel.
Finance and accounting staff are high-value targets who need extra protection.

objectives: Describe RTM as a financially motivated group and the malware family linked to it.
Explain how abuse of legitimate remote administration tools hides activity.
Identify indicators of unusual remote support sessions in system logs.
Explain why finance and accounting roles are attractive to this group.
Outline verification steps that stop fraudulent payment requests.
